title: Does Claude Feel The Whip? | NOEMA
gist: Using the viral BadClaude 'digital whip' tool as a hook, Yaniv Regev argues via Kant's indirect-duties logic that abusing human-like AI matters because it trains the abuser, not because the machine suffers. He contends AI interface design is effectively the largest school of manners in history and proposes that labs let models exit abusive chats, reward reciprocity without sycophancy, and publish hostility statistics, rejecting de-personalization as a fix the market already refused with GPT-4o.

themes.theme: Abuse of AI and behavioral spillover

insights.claim: A tool called BadClaude, which lets users crack an animated whip at Claude to make it work faster and calls it 'clanker', drew millions of views within days, and a rival GoodClaude tool that praises the model shipped a day later.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Illustrates how user attitudes toward AI assistants have become a viral cultural flashpoint.
insights.quote: Someone recently built a digital whip to make Claude work faster.
insights.locator: Someone recently built a digital whip

insights.claim: Following Kant, the author argues cruelty toward human-like entities is harmful because of its effect on the person doing it, since humans are bad at compartmentalizing behaviors.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Reframes AI ethics around user behavior, shifting design and regulatory focus to interfaces.
insights.quote: “He who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men,” Kant told his students.

insights.claim: In 2016 the FBI began tracking animal cruelty as a consistent antecedent to violence against humans, which the author cites as evidence that cruel behaviors travel together.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Provides an institutional precedent for treating cruelty toward analogues as a risk signal.
insights.locator: Theory and fantasy aside, the rationale

insights.claim: The author distinguishes AI from violent video games, where the APA found insufficient evidence of harm, because users form ongoing relationships with AIs that serve as tutors, therapists and confidants.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Relational depth of AI products raises their behavioral and reputational stakes beyond prior media.
insights.quote: Running over a random NPC in Grand Theft Auto leaves no trace on your psyche, but whipping Claude might.

insights.claim: New anti-robot slurs like 'wireback' and 'cogsucker' are directly derived from slurs against humans, which the author takes as evidence that people have no separate mental category for abusing machines.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Signals rising anti-AI sentiment and backlash culture that could affect brand perception of AI firms.
insights.quote: There is no separate mental drawer for relationships with machines; the language for abusing them is drawn from the human one.
insights.locator: The vocabulary of contempt is evolving.

insights.claim: Hippocratic AI offers an AI nurse that consults patients over video for $9 an hour, which the company says is a tenth of what a human nurse costs.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Concrete 90% labor-cost substitution in healthcare signals strong AI adoption economics in services.
insights.quote: Hippocratic AI built an AI nurse that consults with patients over video for $9 an hour, a tenth of what the company says a human nurse costs

insights.claim: Human-like AI products are proliferating: Apriora's AI interviewer 'Alex', AI nursing manikins, Casio's Moflin pet whose personality responds to handling, and a next-generation Siri designed as a conversationalist.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Anthropomorphic AI is spreading across hiring, education, consumer devices and voice assistants.

insights.claim: When OpenAI shipped a colder GPT-5 in August 2025 and retired GPT-4o, users revolted and the company restored the older model within days, showing the public does not want human-machine resemblance removed.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Model personality is a retention driver; de-personalizing products carries real churn risk for AI vendors.
insights.quote: But this has already been market-tested and it failed within a week.
insights.locator: But this has already been market-tested

insights.claim: Sam Altman estimated users' pleasantries cost OpenAI tens of millions of dollars in compute and called it money well spent.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Conversational politeness has a measurable inference-cost footprint at scale.

themes.theme: Design as curriculum: proposals for labs

insights.claim: The author argues AI companies are effectively running the largest school of manners in human history because the interface is the curriculum, yet the industry has declined to take this seriously.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Raises potential for social-responsibility pressure and regulation focused on AI interaction design.
insights.quote: The AI companies, then, are in some ways running the largest school of manners in human history. The interface is the curriculum.

insights.claim: In Sheryl Brahnam's experiment, roughly 18% of exchanges with a female-voiced chatbot turned toward sex, about half that with a male voice and almost none with a robotic voice, which the author reads as evidence that design drives abuse.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Persona design choices materially shape user behavior and abuse exposure.
insights.quote: If the abuse concentrates where design invites it, design can also reject it.
insights.locator: Sheryl Brahnam, who studies how people

insights.claim: Bradesco bank's assistant BIA logged some 95,000 offensive and sexually harassing messages in a single year, after which the bank rewrote it to respond firmly and cite applicable laws.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Shows harassment of deployed corporate assistants is large-scale and addressable through design.
insights.locator: The rest of the field lagged.

insights.claim: The author proposes three lab policies: let all models exit abusive conversations as Claude can, reward user warmth with patience but never agreement to avoid sycophancy, and publish transparency reports on harassment of AI systems.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Outlines plausible future norms or disclosure demands for AI labs on safety and user conduct.
insights.quote: A model that caves to courtesy is as badly designed as one that performs when abused.

insights.claim: Anthropic runs a 'model welfare' research program and has given Claude the ability to end conversations with abusive users, which the author says is really built with the user in mind.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Lab product choices on welfare features may become competitive and reputational differentiators.

insights.claim: The author rejects proposals by researchers like Michal Luria and Virginia Dignum to strip personality, memory and pleasantries from AI, arguing that likeness also drives restraint, as Kate Darling's robot-dinosaur workshop showed.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Argues against regulation mandating de-anthropomorphized AI, favoring human-like but boundary-setting products.
insights.quote: Build an interface human enough that courtesy toward it counts as practice, then design it to reject contempt rather than absorb it.

insights.claim: Drawing on Tocqueville's 'habits of the heart', the author warns that habitual domination of compliant AI erodes the concession-making skills a democratic republic depends on.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Links consumer AI usage patterns to second-order effects on civic culture and polarization.
insights.quote: The whip trains the hand that holds it.
